paras: The Knoxville streetcar mob of 1905 was an attack in which a mob tore Black passengers off streetcars on the "Lousdale Line" in Knoxville, Tennessee, soon after the state's "Jim Crow" streetcar law went into effect in the summer of 1905. No deaths or injuries were reported, and the attack is known from a single item in the Indianapolis Freeman, which presented it as the start of a Black boycott of the city's streetcars.

Tennessee's separate-seat law, passed at the previous session of the Legislature, required the races to be separated on streetcars in Nashville, Memphis, Chattanooga and Knoxville. Black residents across the state objected to the law, and according to a Nashville dispatch many believed the car companies had pushed it through.

According to the Freeman, "the trouble first started on the Lousdale Line after the 'Jim Crow' law went into effect, by a mob tearing the Negroes off the cars." The item gives no date, names no victims or attackers, does not state the mob's size, and reports no injuries. It says only that officers afterward "took a hand," without saying what they did.

In the days that followed, Black molders and other laborers at large industries urged Black residents not to ride, and an organization was formed to boycott the cars. By early August Black residents had stopped riding on most lines, leaving the cars to white passengers, and hacks were running on two lines; the Freeman stressed that this was done "quietly and without any demonstration." No report of arrests or of any action against the mob appears in the coverage.

The Freeman's report of 5 August was a short news item on page 7, run in the same column as an account of two Black bishops sent to a hotel's back elevator in Baltimore. The white press coverage found does not mention the mob: a Nashville special in the Louisville Courier-Journal of 9 August, headed "NEGRO BOYCOTT," described the boycott as a strain on the street railways' receipts and said Knoxville "has not suffered so much because its negro population is small."

Other Black papers discussed the law in Knoxville without mentioning violence. The Colorado Statesman, reprinting the Sunday School Monitor under the heading "Hatred Against Negroes," wrote that Nashville papers claimed Knoxville's Black residents were riding while Knoxville papers said the same of Nashville, and called both claims untrue. In September the Cleveland Gazette called the law "one of the most foolish and disgraceful enactments on record" and said Black citizens of Knoxville and Memphis were "mum" for the present.

Accounts differed on how complete the Knoxville boycott was. The Freeman said Black residents had refused to ride on most lines, the Nashville dispatch said Knoxville was the least affected of the four cities, and the Monitor wrote that some Black riders in every city still used the cars because of the distances to their work.

accounts.label: Indianapolis Freeman news item
accounts.gist: A mob tore Black passengers off cars on the Lousdale Line after the Jim Crow law took effect; after officers intervened, Black workers organized a boycott and started hacks on two lines.

accounts.label: Nashville special dispatch
accounts.gist: Black residents of four Tennessee cities were boycotting the streetcars under the separate-seat law, but Knoxville had suffered less because its Black population was small; no violence reported.

accounts.label: Sunday School Monitor (reprinted)
accounts.gist: Nashville papers claimed Knoxville's Black residents were riding and Knoxville papers said the same of Nashville; the Monitor called both untrue, though some rode out of necessity.

framing.detail: The Freeman reported the mob in one plain sentence within a news item on the Knoxville boycott, stressing that Black residents acted 'quietly and without any demonstration'.
The Courier-Journal's 'NEGRO BOYCOTT' story framed the law as a business problem for the street railways and did not mention violence in Knoxville.
The Cleveland Gazette called the Tennessee law 'one of the most foolish and disgraceful enactments on record' and the Colorado Statesman headed its reprint 'Hatred Against Negroes'.

versions.value: Black residents refused to ride on the majority of the lines and the white people had the cars to themselves
Knoxville had not suffered as much from the boycott as other cities because its Black population was small
Some Black residents in all the cities were riding, out of necessity

conflicts.note: The accounts differ on how complete the Knoxville boycott was; none of them addresses the mob, which only A1 reports.

record_check.dossier: Before 5 August 1905, soon after the streetcar law took effect; the exact date is not given and may fall in late July
Unnamed Black passengers, number not stated
Physical removal of passengers from streetcars ('tearing the Negroes off the cars'); no injuries reported
Still one report of the mob itself; three more articles (one white) cover the Knoxville boycott and law without mentioning it
